claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are solid, single-phase Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy alloys.
Premelting and melting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are governed by internal lattice strain combined with limited atomic mobility.
Atomic-size mismatch among the five constituent metals produces internal lattice strain.
Atomic mobility is limited within these Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles.
Atomic-size mismatch gives rise to chemical heterogeneity within the nanoparticles.
High-strain regions undergo an earlier transition to a quasi-liquid state than the rest of the nanoparticle.
Upon further heating, localized liquid-like regions expand and ultimately produce complete melting.
In situ microscopy and diffraction will show liquid-like behavior beginning in regions of high lattice strain before uniform melting.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles will exhibit a two-stage melting process consisting of localized premelting followed by full melting.
Monometallic or binary baseline nanoparticles have less atomic-size mismatch and lower lattice strain than the five-element HEA nanoparticles.
Monometallic or binary baseline nanoparticles exhibit more uniform, single-stage melting.
Controlled thermal ramping in an inert atmosphere can be used to test the proposed premelting mechanism.
The proposed mechanism applies under conditions that avoid oxidation and competing decomposition reactions.
The proposed mechanism is limited to the nanoscale regime, typically particle sizes below 100 nm.
Finite-size and strain effects are prominent below 100 nm.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticle formation can depend on controlled cooling and inhibited mobility.
Absence of spatial correlation between local strain and premelting onset, or observation of spatially uniform melting without premelting, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
